metadata.title: Predictive insights into U.S. students’ mathematics performance on PISA 2022 using ensemble tree-based machine learning models

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2022 microdata for the United States and merges student and school files using the school identifier (CNTSCHID), then assigns school-level predictors to students within the same school. The analytic sample is restricted to 15-year-old students with available derived variables after cleaning and imputation steps. Although the authors note that PISA provides sampling weights and cite guidance on weighting, they explicitly do not include sampling weights in the ML analyses, arguing that weighting may be less critical for ML model configuration and that ML can still produce reliable results under complex multistage clustered designs. As a result, the models are trained and evaluated without complex survey weighting, which may affect generalizability and uncertainty quantification relative to weight-aware estimation.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Analyzed PISA 2022 data for the United States (15-year-old students). Student and school questionnaires were merged using CNTSCHID so that school-level predictors were assigned to students within the same school. Predictors were cleaned in multiple steps: (1) removed predictors with >50% missing values; (2) removed identical predictors with the exact same values for all students; (3) removed redundant predictors to avoid collinearity (e.g., retained ESCS and excluded its component DVs HISEI, PAREDINT, HOMEPOS); (4) imputed remaining missing predictor values using missForest (RF-based imputation); (5) split the cleaned dataset into training (80%, N=3644) and test (20%, N=908). The outcome was modeled using all 10 PISA math plausible values (PV1MATH–PV10MATH), fitting separate models per PV and averaging results across PVs.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Model comparison using reduced predictor sets: Random Forest (5 predictors) rMSE=69.82, training time=129.27 s; XGBoost (10 predictors) rMSE=66.39, training time=4.14 s; LightGBM (10 predictors) rMSE=66.36, training time=22.93 s. Best model by accuracy+efficiency: XGBoost with rMSE=66.39 and shortest training time (4.14 s). Predictor-selection criterion: ARE threshold 0.1 (reduced model close to full model).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 United States the study leveraged Mathematics self-efficacy, socioeconomic status (ESCS), familiarity with math concepts, expected occupation status, and family support for self-learning to predict mathematics achievement (PVs), finding that XGBoost achieved lower prediction error than Random Forest and slightly lower error than LightGBM while also being much faster to train. This indicates that data-driven, ensemble-tree predictor selection can identify a compact set of actionable correlates of math performance for U.S. students, with self-efficacy and ESCS emerging as consistently top signals, though the results are predictive (not causal) and were obtained without sampling weights.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzed PISA 2022 mathematics achievement for U.S. 15-year-olds (N=4552 in 154 schools) and predicted PV-based math performance using three ensemble tree models: Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM. After cleaning predictors (dropping >50% missing predictors, removing identical/redundant variables) and imputing remaining missing values with missForest, the authors trained models separately for each of the 10 math plausible values (PV1MATH–PV10MATH) and averaged results across PVs. Model performance was compared using reduced-model rMSE (full vs selected predictors) and training time; XGBoost was selected as best overall with rMSE=66.39 and training time=4.14 s (vs RF rMSE=69.82, 129.27 s; LightGBM rMSE=66.36, 22.93 s). The most influential predictors included mathematics self-efficacy and ESCS, plus familiarity with math concepts and family learning support. Limitations include omission of sampling weights and reliance on predictive associations interpreted via ALE (predictive importance ≠ causality).
